implementation_notes: .NET has a specific and very common form of this smell that is worth naming separately: using LINQ-to-Objects where the data is in the database, so the whole table is materialised, or using `ToList()` to satisfy a type constraint before anyone measured the cost. The second is `async`/`await` applied to every I/O call for a reason that was never a bottleneck, which adds state machines and context-switch overhead. The third is structural — a data structure chosen for speed (`int[]` instead of `List<int>`) with no allocation measurement. The tools are `BenchmarkDotNet` and the built-in profilers.
idiom_name: LINQ-to-Objects instead of LINQ-to-Entities; premature async/await
pitfalls: `ToList()` to satisfy a return type is the most common LINQ performance bug and is usually found late.
A missing `AsNoTracking()` in EF Core turns a read-only query into tracked entities, which is a real cost and a configuration choice, not an optimisation.
Making everything async because the code looks better, adding state machines to code that was not an I/O bottleneck.
Benchmarking in Debug configuration, which measures nothing useful.
